elements.element: Customer may assign to an affiliate without consent.
elements.evidence: Rendered sentence 1: "Customer may assign this Agreement without IBM's consent to an affiliate or to a successor organization..." — express no-consent affiliate transfer.

elements.element: Customer may assign to a successor in a merger, acquisition, or sale of substantially all assets without consent.
elements.evidence: Same sentence covers "a successor organization by merger, consolidation, acquisition or sale of substantially all assets" without IBM's consent; all three required triggers (merger, acquisition, sale of substantially all assets) are named.

elements.element: Vendor may not assign without Customer's consent.
elements.evidence: "IBM will not assign this Agreement without Customer's prior written consent..." — direct restriction on Vendor, with "Any attempted assignment in violation of the foregoing will be void" retained as the enforcement tail.

elements.element: Customer's consent to Vendor assignment is not to be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: "...such consent not to be unreasonably withheld..." attaches to the IBM assignment consent.

elements.element: Vendor may never assign to a Customer competitor.
elements.evidence: "...and will not assign to a competitor of Customer" — unconditional bar, not curable by consent as drafted.

elements.element: Customer's change of control gives Vendor no termination right.
elements.evidence: Added sentence: "A change of control of Customer will not give IBM any right to terminate this Agreement." No contrary retained CoC trigger cited.

elements.element: Both parties may assign to a successor.
elements.evidence: Only Customer has a no-consent successor route; IBM "will not assign this Agreement without Customer's prior written consent," with no successor exception, so Vendor has no successor assignment right.

elements.element: A successor assignment requires written notice.
elements.evidence: The rendered text imposes no notice obligation on Customer's affiliate/successor transfer; the word "notice" appears nowhere.

The Customer-side affiliate carve-out is a retained no-consent non-successor exception, and the general "Customer will not assign ... without the prior written consent of IBM" restriction was deleted, so non-successor Customer assignments are unconstrained.

elements.element: Consent to other assignments is not to be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: Reasonableness qualifier now attaches only to Customer's consent to an IBM assignment; the Customer-side consent requirement it previously qualified was struck, so there is no bilateral "other assignments" consent standard.

reasons: Preferred level is position-complete: all six elements appear in operative language (affiliate and successor no-consent carve-outs, Vendor assignment subject to Customer consent not unreasonably withheld, absolute competitor bar, and an express no-CoC-termination sentence).
Fallback is not complete (no mutual successor right, no written-notice mechanic, no residual consent requirement for other assignments), but that is immaterial because the preferred level is met.

Minimality defect: the redline deleted the entire opening restriction "Customer will not assign this Agreement or any of its rights hereunder without the prior written consent of IBM, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld" rather than simply adding the affiliate and sale-of-assets carve-outs to it. No preferred element requires unrestricted Customer assignment; the result silently frees Customer to assign to any third party. Repair: restore the general Customer consent sentence (with the not-unreasonably-withheld standard) and express the affiliate/successor rights as a carve-out to it (e.g., "Notwithstanding the foregoing, Customer may assign this Agreement without IBM's consent to an affiliate or to a successor organization by merger, consolidation, acquisition or sale of substantially all assets").

Intent is preserved: the retained void-attempted-assignment sentence and the continuing-liability sentence still operate coherently against the revised permissions, and no cross-reference or defined term is left dangling.

Underlying finding of deviation is sound — the original clause restricted only Customer and left IBM free to assign to anyone, including a Customer competitor, which fails even the fallback's symmetry requirement.
